items.stem: ‘The Holocaust was the result of Hitler's long-term intention.’ Discuss.
items.answer: For: Hitler's antisemitism was central and consistent. The 1939 prophecy linked war to the annihilation of the Jews. Key escalations, such as the decisions of 1941, required his approval. Against: Policy shifted from emigration to expulsion to murder. Local initiatives drove killing in the occupied east. Competition between agencies radicalised policy. Judgement: Hitler's ideology set the goal and his approval was essential, but the path to genocide was not a long-planned blueprint.

items.stem: ‘The Holocaust was the result of cumulative radicalisation within the Nazi system.’ How far do you agree with this view?
items.answer: For: Policy shifted as earlier solutions failed. Rival agencies competed to show zeal. Local initiatives in the occupied east escalated killing. Against: Hitler's ideology defined the Jews as the enemy. Hitler's approval was needed for key decisions. The radicalisation always moved in one direction, set by ideology. Judgement: cumulative radicalisation explains how the Holocaust developed, but not why its target was the Jews, which requires Hitler's ideology.

items.stem: ‘Ordinary perpetrators of the Holocaust killed mainly because of situational pressures rather than ideology.’ Discuss.
items.answer: For: Few stepped out when given the chance at Józefów. Conformity and peer pressure were powerful. Many perpetrators were not Nazi activists. Against: Antisemitic propaganda shaped attitudes. Some killed with enthusiasm beyond orders. Non-Germans also killed, suggesting varied motives including ideology and opportunism. Judgement: situational pressures explain why most ordinary men took part, but ideology defined who the victims were and made killing acceptable.

Rival agencies competed to solve the "Jewish question". Local officials in the east began killing on their own initiative. The failure of expulsion plans such as Madagascar created pressure for a "solution". No written order from Hitler exists. [2]

items.stem: Nadia is planning an answer to the question: “‘The Holocaust was the result of cumulative radicalisation within the Nazi system.’ How far do you agree?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Nadia could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: cumulative radicalisation explains how the Holocaust developed, but not why its target was the Jews, which requires Hitler's ideology. Support: Policy shifted as earlier solutions failed. Rival agencies competed to show zeal. Challenge: Hitler's ideology defined the Jews as the enemy. Hitler's approval was needed for key decisions.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: How far did the war against the Soviet Union transform Nazi policy towards the Jews?
items.answer: For: Einsatzgruppen began mass shootings in 1941. Millions of Jews came under German control. The war of annihilation removed restraints. Against: Persecution had grown steadily since 1933. Ghettos in Poland already caused mass deaths. Ideology made Jews the target before the war. Judgement: the war against the USSR was the decisive turning point from persecution to genocide, but it radicalised an existing ideological aim.

Level 4 (13-16): analysis of both sides with a judgement, though not fully sustained or supported. Level 3 (9-12): some analysis, but one-sided or uneven, or with descriptive passages. Level 2 (5-8): mainly descriptive or narrative, with limited links to the question. Level 1 (1-4): general, unsupported or irrelevant points. Ideology made Jews the target before the war. Possible judgement: the war against the USSR was the decisive turning point from persecution to genocide, but it radicalised an existing ideological aim. items.stem: Read the extract and then answer the question. Extract: a historian writing in the 1970s (illustrative). “The Third Reich was not a monolith but a jungle of competing agencies. Gauleiters, the SS, the ministries and the occupation authorities each pursued their own answer to a "Jewish question" that the regime had defined but never solved. When expulsion proved impossible, the deportations jammed and the ghettos overflowed, officials improvised the solution of murder.” What can you learn from this extract about the interpretation and approach of the historian who wrote it? Use the extract and your knowledge of the Holocaust to explain your answer.
items.answer: Interpretation: The Holocaust emerged through cumulative radicalisation within a chaotic, competitive system rather than from a plan. Approach: The historian focuses on the structures of the Nazi state and how decisions were made, rather than on Hitler's ideas. Own knowledge that supports it: Rival agencies competed for power. Expulsion plans such as Madagascar failed. Local officials began gassings at Chełmno in December 1941. Own knowledge that challenges it: Hitler's statements and prophecy show intent. Himmler reported to Hitler and acted with his authority. Antisemitic ideology was central from 1933. Context: West German historians such as Martin Broszat and Hans Mommsen developed this view in the 1970s using the records of the Nazi administration.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): demonstrates a full understanding of the historian's interpretation and approach, explained with close reference to the extract and tested against accurate own knowledge. Level 4 (13-16): explains the main interpretation with support from the extract and shows some understanding of the approach. Level 3 (9-12): identifies the main interpretation with some support, or explains sub-messages. Level 2 (5-8): identifies sub-messages or makes valid points about the topic linked to the extract. Level 1 (1-4): paraphrases or summarises the extract, or writes about the topic without reference to it. (The examination question is marked out of 40; levels are scaled.) [20]

items.stem: In a revision class, a student says: “Collaborators in occupied countries took part in the Holocaust.” Is this accurate? Explain your answer using your own knowledge.
items.answer: Accurate. For example, local police in France and auxiliary units in the Baltic states and Ukraine.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a correct judgement; 1 mark for accurate supporting knowledge [2]

items.stem: Analyse the reasons why ordinary men became killers.
items.answer: Conformity and unwillingness to break ranks with comrades. Obedience to authority and fear of appearing weak. Antisemitic propaganda dehumanised victims. Brutalisation by war and the division of labour in killing. Careerism and opportunism. Judgement: situational pressures explain why most took part, though ideology shaped how they saw their victims.
items.markingKey: Level 4 (9-10): analyses a range of factors, showing how they interact, with a supported judgement on their relative importance. Level 3 (6-8): explains two or more factors with accurate support. Level 2 (3-5): describes or identifies factors, or explains one. Level 1 (1-2): general points. Indicative content: Conformity and unwillingness to break ranks with comrades. Obedience to authority and fear of appearing weak. Antisemitic propaganda dehumanised victims. Brutalisation by war and the division of labour in killing. Careerism and opportunism. Possible judgement: situational pressures explain why most took part, though ideology shaped how they saw their victims. [10]

items.stem: Ana is planning an answer to the question: “‘Ordinary perpetrators of the Holocaust killed mainly because of situational pressures rather than ideology.’ How far do you agree?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Ana could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: situational pressures explain why most ordinary men took part, but ideology defined who the victims were and made killing acceptable. Support: Few stepped out when given the chance at Józefów. Conformity and peer pressure were powerful. Challenge: Antisemitic propaganda shaped attitudes. Some killed with enthusiasm beyond orders.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: Tariq is planning an answer to the question: “How far has the debate between intentionalists and functionalists been resolved by a synthesis?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Tariq could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: a synthesis has largely replaced the old polarised debate, but disagreements over timing and emphasis remain. Support: Most historians now combine ideology and structure. Kershaw's "working towards the Führer" links both. Challenge: Debates continue over when and how decisions were taken. The perpetrator debate raised new questions.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: The following extract is from a historian writing in the 1980s (illustrative). “To ask whether Hitler planned the Holocaust is to ask the wrong question. The regime set itself an impossible aim, a Germany "free of Jews", and every failure to achieve it by deportation increased the pressure for more radical measures. The bureaucracy did not need orders; it needed only a goal.” How far does your own knowledge support the interpretation in the extract? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Supporting evidence: Deportation plans repeatedly failed. Rival agencies sought radical solutions. Ghettos created crises officials tried to solve. Challenging evidence: Hitler's statements show intent. Key decisions in 1941 involved Hitler. Ideology defined the goal. Judgement: the interpretation is supported in part; its strength depends on the evidence it emphasises.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the interpretation; up to 3 marks for own knowledge that supports it and up to 3 for knowledge that challenges it, each linked to the extract; 1 mark for a supported judgement [8]

items.stem: Read the extract and then answer the question. Extract: a historian writing in the 1970s (illustrative). “From the pages of Mein Kampf to the bunker in Berlin, Hitler's hatred of the Jews was the one constant of his career. The Final Solution was not an accident of war or a product of rivalry between officials. It was the fulfilment of a purpose that Hitler had announced openly, and which he pursued step by step as circumstances allowed.” Which of these best describes the approach of the historian who wrote the extract?
options: Focus on the behaviour and motives of individual perpetrators
Focus on Hitler's ideology and statements
Focus on collaborators and bystanders across occupied Europe
Focus on local initiatives in the occupied territories
items.answer: Focus on Hitler's ideology and statements
items.markingKey: The historian focuses on Hitler's ideology and statements, tracing a straight line from his early writings to genocide. [1]

items.stem: Mei is planning an answer to the question: “How far does the lack of a written order from Hitler weaken the intentionalist interpretation?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Mei could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: the lack of an order weakens claims of a long-term plan, but not the argument that Hitler's ideology and approval were essential. Support: It removes direct proof of a plan. It fits functionalist evidence of improvised decisions. Challenge: Hitler often gave oral orders. Himmler and others referred to the Führer's wishes.

items.stem: No written order from Hitler for the "Final Solution" has been found. How far does the lack of a written order from Hitler weaken the intentionalist interpretation?

Judgement: the lack of an order weakens claims of a long-term plan, but not the argument that Hitler's ideology and approval were essential.

items.stem: What is meant by “cumulative radicalisation”?

The Nazi term for the plan to murder all the Jews of Europe.
Hans Mommsen's term for the process by which competing agencies drove policy to ever more extreme measures.
Non-Germans in occupied or allied countries who assisted the Nazi persecution.

items.stem: Read the extract and then answer the question. Extract: a historian writing in 1999 (illustrative). “In the occupied east in the summer of 1941 the killing spread from Jewish men of military age to women and children. The decisive steps were often taken by commanders on the spot, competing to show their zeal and reporting their "successes" to Berlin. Policy was made as much in the occupied cities of the east as in the Reich Chancellery.” What can you learn from this extract about the interpretation and approach of the historian who wrote it? Use the extract and your knowledge of the Holocaust to explain your answer.
items.answer: Interpretation: Radicalisation came from initiatives in the occupied territories as much as from orders from the centre. Approach: The historian focuses on local initiatives in the occupied territories, using regional records. Own knowledge that supports it: Einsatzgruppen reports show competition in numbers killed. Killing of women and children spread from late July and August 1941. Babi Yar, September 1941, was organised locally with the army. Own knowledge that challenges it: Himmler toured the east and encouraged escalation. The killing was consistent with Hitler's ideological war. Central decisions were needed for deportations from the Reich.

items.stem: Study the extract. “Officials across the Reich worked towards the Führer: they anticipated what Hitler wanted and competed to deliver it. Hitler set the ideological direction and gave his approval at crucial moments; the initiatives and the radicalism came from below. Neither intention nor structure alone explains the Holocaust.” (A historian writing in 1998 (illustrative).) What can you learn from this extract about the interpretation and approach of the historian who wrote it? Use the extract and your knowledge of the Holocaust to explain your answer.
items.answer: Interpretation: Hitler's ideology and approval were essential, but cumulative radicalisation by officials working towards his wishes drove the process. Approach: The historian combines analysis of Hitler's role with the structures of the regime, explaining how his authority worked through the system. Own knowledge that supports it: Hitler's approval was sought for deportations from the Reich in autumn 1941. Officials competed to fulfil his wishes. Ideological goals were clear but methods were improvised. Own knowledge that challenges it: Intentionalists argue Hitler planned more directly. Goldhagen stressed ordinary Germans' motives. Some decisions may have come entirely from the centre.

items.stem: The following extract is from a historian writing in 1996 (illustrative). “The perpetrators were willing. They killed with zeal, photographed their deeds and sent the pictures home. Such conduct cannot be explained by obedience or peer pressure. It sprang from a conviction, long rooted in German culture, that the Jews were a dangerous enemy who deserved to be eliminated.” What is the main interpretation of the historian in the extract? Support your answer with two details from the extract.
items.answer: Interpretation: Ordinary Germans were willing executioners motivated by a long-standing eliminationist antisemitism. Support from the extract: for example, “The perpetrators were willing.”

items.stem: Leila is planning an answer to the question: “How far does the study of collaborators and bystanders change our understanding of the Holocaust?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Leila could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: it widens our understanding of how the Holocaust was carried out, but not of why it was decided upon. items.stem: Consider the following explanations of why interpretations of the Holocaust have changed over time. A: Debates between schools refined arguments. B: New evidence, such as Eastern European archives, became available. C: The political context of the Cold War and of German memory changed. Explain which of these was the most important reason.
items.answer: Any reasoned choice. A: Debates between schools refined arguments. B: New evidence, such as Eastern European archives, became available. C: The political context of the Cold War and of German memory changed. Possible judgement: new evidence and new questions, shaped by changing contexts, explain the development of the debate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a choice; up to 3 marks for explaining it with precise detail; up to 2 marks for comparing it with the other reasons [6]

items.stem: The following extract is from a historian writing in 2004 (illustrative). “The new evidence from the archives of the east shows decisions taken in stages in the second half of 1941, each approved by Hitler and each more radical than the last. Hitler was not the author of every initiative, but nothing of significance happened without him.” How far does your own knowledge support the interpretation in the extract? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Supporting evidence: Mass shootings escalated in summer 1941. Deportations from the Reich were approved in autumn 1941. Death camps were built from late 1941. Challenging evidence: Intentionalists see a plan earlier. Functionalists stress local initiatives more. The exact date of a decision remains disputed. Judgement: the interpretation is supported in part; its strength depends on the evidence it emphasises.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the interpretation; up to 3 marks for own knowledge that supports it and up to 3 for knowledge that challenges it, each linked to the extract; 1 mark for a supported judgement [8]
